```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Build the cleaned file from the raw data if it is not there yet
clean_path <- here("data", "spotify_tracks_clean.csv")
if (!file.exists(clean_path)) {
  owd <- setwd(here())
  source(here("R", "01_get_data.R"))
  setwd(owd)
}
songs <- read_csv(clean_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

dir.create(here("figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
source_note <- "Source: Spotify Tracks Dataset, Maharshi Pandya (Kaggle / Hugging Face)"
```

```{r}
#| label: numbers
n_songs    <- nrow(songs)
n_genres   <- n_distinct(songs$track_genre)
r_all      <- cor(songs$danceability, songs$popularity)
share_zero <- mean(songs$popularity == 0)

# Mean popularity in five danceability bins
bins <- songs |>
  mutate(dance_bin = cut(danceability, breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2),
                         include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(dance_bin) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_pop = mean(popularity), .groups = "drop")
bin_text <- paste0(round(bins$mean_pop, 1), " (",
                   c("0-0.2", "0.2-0.4", "0.4-0.6", "0.6-0.8", "0.8-1"), ")",
                   collapse = ", ")

dance0 <- songs |> filter(danceability == 0)
n_dance0_sleep <- sum(dance0$track_genre == "sleep")

# Genre alone: share of the variation in each variable
r2_dance_genre <- summary(lm(danceability ~ track_genre, data = songs))$r.squared
r2_pop_genre   <- summary(lm(popularity ~ track_genre, data = songs))$r.squared

pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(round(100 * x, d), "%")
```

Our question is whether a song's danceability is associated with its
popularity on Spotify, and whether that association holds among songs of the
same genre. We use the Spotify Tracks Dataset, collected from the Spotify Web
API (see `data/codebook.md`). The raw file has 114,000 rows, but the same song
appears many times: under several genres, and as copies on compilation albums
(for example, Imagine Dragons' "Thunder" on "Halloween Party 2022"). These
copies usually have popularity 0 even when the original is a hit. We keep one
row per song (same title and artists), the version with the highest
popularity, which leaves **`r format(n_songs, big.mark = ",")` songs in
`r n_genres` genres**. The two figures below set up the two steps of our
planned analysis: the overall relationship (H1) and the comparison within
genre (H2).

## Figure 1. Danceability and popularity, all songs

```{r}
#| label: overall-plot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8

fig1 <- ggplot(songs, aes(x = danceability, y = popularity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"),
              colour = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(subtitle = paste0("One point per song (n = ", format(n_songs, big.mark = ","),
                         "); red line = smooth trend"),
       x = "Danceability (0 = least, 1 = most danceable)",
       y = "Popularity (0-100)",
       caption = source_note)

fig1
ggsave(here("figures", "fig1_danceability_popularity.png"), fig1,
       width = 7, height = 3.8, dpi = 300)
```

**What it shows.** The relationship is weak: the correlation between
danceability and popularity is `r sprintf("%.2f", r_all)`. Average popularity by
danceability bin is `r bin_text`. So popularity rises from the least danceable
songs to the middle of the range and then levels off, with a small drop for the
most danceable songs. At every danceability level, popularity is very spread
out, from 0 to over 90. Even after removing the compilation copies,
`r pct(share_zero, 1)` of songs have popularity exactly 0 (the dark row along
the bottom). The upturn at the far left rests on only `r nrow(dance0)` songs
with danceability exactly 0, and `r n_dance0_sleep` of them are from the
"sleep" genre (white noise and sleep sounds), not ordinary songs.

**Why it matters.** Danceability alone explains very little of a song's
popularity, so H1 (more danceable songs are more popular) is only weakly
supported at first look. Because the trend rises and then levels off rather
than following a straight line, we plan to test a quadratic term in the
regression. The songs at popularity 0 may still distort the fit, so we will
repeat the analysis without them. Since the overall link is so weak, Figure 2
checks whether it differs by genre.

## Figure 2. Danceability and popularity within genre

```{r}
#| label: genre-numbers
genres_to_show <- c("pop", "dance", "hip-hop", "classical", "ambient", "rock")

genre_stats <- songs |>
  filter(track_genre %in% genres_to_show) |>
  group_by(track_genre) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_pop = mean(popularity),
            share0 = mean(popularity == 0),
            slope = coef(lm(popularity ~ danceability))[2],
            slope_no0 = coef(lm(popularity ~ danceability,
                                data = pick(everything()) |> filter(popularity > 0)))[2],
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(slope))

g <- function(genre, col) genre_stats[[col]][genre_stats$track_genre == genre]
sl <- function(genre) sprintf("%+.1f", g(genre, "slope"))

strip_labels <- setNames(paste0(genre_stats$track_genre, " (n = ", genre_stats$n, ")"),
                         genre_stats$track_genre)
```

```{r}
#| label: genre-plot
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5

fig2 <- songs |>
  filter(track_genre %in% genres_to_show) |>
  mutate(track_genre = factor(track_genre, levels = genre_stats$track_genre)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = danceability, y = popularity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ track_genre, labeller = as_labeller(strip_labels)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(subtitle = "Six genres, one point per song; red line = linear fit",
       x = "Danceability (0-1)",
       y = "Popularity (0-100)",
       caption = source_note) +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"))

fig2
ggsave(here("figures", "fig2_within_genre.png"), fig2,
       width = 7.5, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

**What it shows.** The same relationship is plotted separately for six genres
(panels are ordered from the most positive to the most negative slope). The
direction differs by genre. The fitted slopes (popularity points per +1.0
danceability) are `r sl(genre_stats$track_genre[1])` in
`r genre_stats$track_genre[1]`, `r sl(genre_stats$track_genre[2])` in
`r genre_stats$track_genre[2]`, `r sl(genre_stats$track_genre[3])` in
`r genre_stats$track_genre[3]`, `r sl(genre_stats$track_genre[4])` in
`r genre_stats$track_genre[4]`, `r sl(genre_stats$track_genre[5])` in
`r genre_stats$track_genre[5]`, and `r sl(genre_stats$track_genre[6])` in
`r genre_stats$track_genre[6]`. Genres also differ in average popularity, from
`r round(min(genre_stats$mean_pop), 1)`
(`r genre_stats$track_genre[which.min(genre_stats$mean_pop)]`) to
`r round(max(genre_stats$mean_pop), 1)`
(`r genre_stats$track_genre[which.max(genre_stats$mean_pop)]`). Across all
`r n_genres` genres, genre alone accounts for `r pct(r2_dance_genre)` of the
variation in danceability and `r pct(r2_pop_genre)` of the variation in
popularity, so knowing a song's genre already tells us a lot about both
variables. The panels have different numbers of songs because each song is
kept under one genre only; some genres (for example pop) lose many songs that
are also listed under other genres.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-genre
genre_stats |>
  transmute(Genre = track_genre, Songs = n,
            `Mean popularity` = round(mean_pop, 1),
            `Share at 0` = pct(share0),
            `Slope` = round(slope, 1),
            `Slope without 0s` = round(slope_no0, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Popularity and the danceability slope in the six genres of Figure 2.")
```

The songs at popularity 0 still matter inside some genres (see the table).
When we drop them, several slopes change noticeably, so a straight line fitted
to all songs should be read with care.

**Why it matters.** The overall correlation of `r sprintf("%.2f", r_all)` hides large
differences between genres, which supports H2 that genre matters for the
danceability-popularity link. Because genre is related to both danceability
and popularity, part of the pattern in Figure 1 could come from differences
between genres rather than from danceability itself. For the analysis, this
means we should add genre to the regression
(`popularity ~ danceability + track_genre`), test an interaction between
danceability and genre, and run the robustness check without popularity-0
songs.

## Code and data

The script `R/01_get_data.R` downloads the raw file (kept out of the
repository) and builds the cleaned file `data/spotify_tracks_clean.csv`.
The file `analysis/02_milestone3_figures.qmd` makes both figures and saves
them in `figures/`.
